subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Prospect Theory in Policy
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Prospect Theory in Policy.

hook.text: A carbon tax framed as 'climate action dividend' passes polls. The same tax framed as 'new tax' fails. Same policy.

buildup.text: Policymakers who understand framing design policies that feel like gains, not losses, for the public.

discovery.text: Prospect theory shapes voter behavior. Incumbents run on gains ('look what we achieved'). Challengers run on losses.

twist.text: Loss-framed policies often fail politically even when they're economically sound. Perception beats substance.

climax.text: Good policy isn't enough. It must be framed so citizens feel the gain, not the loss. Communication is policy.

punchline.text: Frame the policy right, or it won't get passed.

quiz.question: Why do some beneficial policies fail to gain public support?
options: The public understands all the details
They're framed as losses rather than gains
All policies eventually get public support

details.summary: Governments use prospect theory to design more effective policies. Tax penalties framed as losses are more motivating then equivalent incentives framed as gains, and default options exploit status quo bias to increase participation in beneficial programs.
details.whyItMatters: Policy design that ignores how people actually make decisions wastes resources and reduces effectiveness. Prospect theory provides tools for designing policies that work with human psychology rather than against it.
takeaways: Loss-framed penalties are more effective than equivalent gain-framed rewards
Default enrollment exploits status quo bias for beneficial programs
Framing policy choices affects public support and compliance

faq.question: How do governments use loss aversion in tax policy?
faq.answer: Framing tax incentives as penalties for non-compliance rather than rewards for compliance dramatically increases response rates. People work harder to avoid losing a tax credit than to earn the same amount as a bonus.

faq.question: What is the most successful prospect theory application in policy?
faq.answer: Automatic enrollment in retirement savings plans. By making participation the default and requiring action to opt out, status quo bias and loss aversion keep people enrolled. This single design change has increased retirement savings by billions.
